en.content: A block A of mass m is placed over a plank B of mass 2m. Plank B is placed over a smooth horizontal surface. The coefficient of friction between A and B is $\frac{1}{2}$. Block A is given a velocity $v_0$ towards right. Acceleration of B relative to A is
en.explanation:
Since block A is moving to the right with velocity $\mathrm{v}_0$ relative to plank B , kinetic friction will act between them to oppose this relative motion.

So, friction will act towards the left on plank A and by Newton's third law, an equal and opposite friction force will act on plank B towards the right.

The ground is smooth, i.e., there is no friction between plank B and the horizontal surface.

The normal force ( N ) acting on block A from plank B must balance the weight of A because there is no vertical motion :

$$ \mathrm{N}=\mathrm{mg} $$

The kinetic friction force (f) acting between the surfaces in contact is,

$$ \mathrm{f}=\mu \mathrm{N} $$

The coefficient of friction is $\mu=\frac{1}{2}$,

$$ \mathrm{f}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \mathrm{mg}=\frac{\mathrm{mg}}{2} $$

Let the direction towards the right be positive ( + ).

For Block A,

The mass of block is $m_A = m$ and the net force acting is $F_A = -f = -\frac{mg}{2}$

Using Newton's Second Law $(F = ma)$,

$$-f = m \cdot a_A \Rightarrow -\frac{mg}{2} = ma_A$$

$$\Rightarrow a_A = -\frac{g}{2}$$

For Block B,

The mass of block is $m_B = m$ and the net force acting is $F_B = +f = \frac{mg}{2}$

Using Newton's Second Law $(F = ma)$,

$$f = 2m \cdot a_B \Rightarrow \frac{mg}{2} = 2ma_B$$

$$\Rightarrow a_B = \frac{g}{4}$$

The acceleration of B relative to A $(a_{BA})$ is,

$$a_{BA} = a_B - a_A$$

Substituting the values:

$$a_{BA} = \frac{g}{4} - \left(-\frac{g}{2}\right) = \frac{3g}{4}$$

Therefore, the acceleration of B relative to A is $\frac{3g}{4}$. Hence, the correct option is (C).

en.content: A block of mass 2 kg is placed on the floor. The coefficient of static and kinetic friction is 0.4. If a force of 2.8 N is applied on the block parallel to floor, the force of friction between the block and floor (taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$) is
en.explanation:
When an object is placed on a rough surface and an external horizontal force is applied, the resistive force friction acts parallel to the contact surface to oppose the relative motion.

In the vertical direction, the a downward gravitational force acts on the block which is equal to its weight $(mg)$.

Since there is no vertical motion, the floor exerts an equal and opposite upward normal force:

$$N = mg$$

When the applied force is low, the body remains at rest. The friction acting in this state is static friction. It is a self-adjusting force that changes its magnitude to balance the applied force.

Static friction has an upper limit beyond which it cannot adjust to balance the external force. This maximum value is called the limiting friction and is proportional to the normal force:

$$f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N$$

where $\mu_s$ is the coefficient of static friction.

If the applied force $(F_{\text{applied}})$ is less than or equal to $f_{s,\max}$, the block stays at rest, and the static friction force is

$$f_s = F_{\text{applied}}$$

If $F_{\text{applied}}$ exceeds $f_{s,\max}$, the block begins to move, and kinetic friction $(f_k = \mu_k N)$ starts acting.

Given the mass $m = 2\,\text{kg}$ and acceleration due to gravity $g = 10\,\text{m}/\text{s}^2$:

$$N = mg$$

$$N = 2 \times 10\,\text{N} = 20\,\text{N}$$

Given the friction coefficient $\mu_s = 0.4$:

$$f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N$$

$$f_{s,\max} = 0.4 \times 20\,\text{N} = 8\,\text{N}$$

The external force is given as $F_{\text{applied}} = 2.8\,\text{N}$ parallel to the floor.

$$2.8\,\text{N} < 8\,\text{N} \Rightarrow F_{\text{applied}} < f_{s,\max}$$

Since the applied force is less than the maximum threshold force required to overcome friction, the block will not move.

Because the block remains stationary, the static friction force must equal the applied force to maintain horizontal equilibrium:

$$f_s = F_{\text{applied}} = 2.8\,\text{N}$$

Therefore, the correct option is (A).

en.content: A body of mass 60 kg is dragged with just enough force to start moving on a rough surface with coefficients of static and kinetic frictions 0.5 and 0.4 respectively. On applying the same force, what is the acceleration? $(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2})$
en.explanation:
For a body to just start moving from rest, the external applied force (F) must balance the maximum possible opposing force at rest, which is the limiting static friction force ( $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{s}, \max }$ )

$$N = mg$$

$$f_{s(\max)} = \mu_s N = \mu_s mg$$

Therefore, the force applied to just start motion is $F = \mu_s mg$

Once the body begins to slide, the friction becomes kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N = \mu_k mg$, where $\mu_k$ is the coefficient of kinetic friction.

According to Newton's second law, $F_{\text{net}} = ma$, where net horizontal force is $F_{\text{net}}$ acting on a body of mass $(m)$ and its acceleration is $(a)$.

$$F - f_k = ma$$

$$\mu_s mg - \mu_k mg = ma$$

$$m(\mu_s - \mu_k)g = ma$$

$$a = (\mu_s - \mu_k)g$$

$$a = (0.5 - 0.4) \times 9.8$$

$$a = 0.1 \times 9.8 = 0.98\,\mathrm{m/s}^2$$

Therefore, the correct option is (A).

en.content: A wooden block of mass M resting on a rough horizontal floor is pulled with a force F at an angle $\phi$ with the horizontal. If $\mu$ is the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface, then acceleration of the block is
en.explanation:
When a force F is applied at an angle $\phi$ to the horizontal,

Horizontal component acting parallel to the floor is $F_x = F\cos\phi$

Vertical component acting vertically upwards is $F_y = F\sin\phi$

Since the block remains on the floor and does not move vertically, the net force in the vertical direction must be zero.

Upward normal reaction force exerted by the ground is $N$

Upward vertical component of the pulling force is $F\sin\phi$

Downward gravitational force (weight of the block) is $Mg$

$$N + F\sin\phi = Mg$$

$$N = Mg - F\sin\phi$$

Friction opposes the relative motion between the block and the floor. The magnitude of kinetic friction force is

$$f_k = \mu N$$

Where $\mu$ is the coefficient of kinetic friction.

$$f_k = \mu (Mg - F\sin\phi)$$

According to Newton's second law of motion,

$$F_{\text{net}} = Ma$$

$$F\cos\phi - f_k = Ma$$

$$F\cos\phi - \mu (Mg - F\sin\phi) = Ma$$

$$F\cos\phi - \mu Mg + \mu F\sin\phi = Ma$$

$$F\cos\phi + \mu F\sin\phi - \mu Mg = Ma$$

$$F(\cos\phi + \mu \sin\phi) - \mu Mg = Ma$$

$$a = \frac{F(\cos\phi + \mu \sin\phi) - \mu Mg}{M}$$

$$a = \frac{F}{M}(\cos\phi + \mu \sin\phi) - \mu g$$

Therefore, the acceleration of the block is $\frac{F}{M}(\cos\phi + \mu \sin\phi) - \mu g$.

Thus, the correct option is (C).

en.content: A given object takes $\sqrt{2}$ times time to slide down $45^{\circ}$ rough inclined plane as it takes to slide down a perfectly smooth $45^{\circ}$ incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the object and the incline is
en.explanation:
Let an inclined plane at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. A block of mass m slides down a distance s along the incline starting from rest (initial velocity $\mathrm{u}=0$ ).

The gravitational force mg acts vertically downward.

The component of gravitational force parallel to the incline is $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{gll}}=\mathrm{mg} \sin \theta$

The component of gravitational force perpendicular to the incline is $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{g} \perp}=\mathrm{mg} \cos \theta$

Since there is no motion perpendicular to the incline surface,

$$\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{mg} \cos \theta ........(i) $$

Case-1 when the surface is smooth

On a perfectly smooth surface, the friction coefficient is zero ( $\mu=0$ ). The only force for the motion down the incline is the component of weight :

$$F_{\text{net}1}=mg\sin\theta$$

Using Newton's second law ($F_{\text{net}1}=ma_1$), the acceleration $a_1$ is:

$$ma_1=mg\sin\theta \Rightarrow a_1=g\sin\theta$$

From the kinematic equation of motion for a given distance $s$ starting from rest ($u=0$):

$$s=ut_1+\frac{1}{2}a_1t_1^2$$

$$s=0+\frac{1}{2}(g\sin\theta)t_1^2 \Rightarrow t_1^2=\frac{2s}{g\sin\theta}\ldots (ii)$$

Case-2 when the surface is rough,

On a rough surface, kinetic friction opposes the downward motion.

$$f_k = \mu N = \mu mg\cos\theta$$

The net force acting down the incline is:

$$F_{\text{net}2} = mg\sin\theta - \mu mg\cos\theta$$

Using Newton's second law

$$ma_2 = mg(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta) \rightarrow a_2 = g(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta)$$

Using the kinematic equation for the same distance $s$ starting from rest:

$$s = \frac{1}{2} a_2 t_2^2 \rightarrow t_2^2 = \frac{2s}{g(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta)} \ldots (\mathrm{iii})$$

It is given that the time taken on the rough incline ($t_2$) is $\sqrt{2}$ times the time taken on the smooth incline ($t_1$):

$$t_2 = \sqrt{2}\,t_1$$

$$t_2^2 = 2t_1^2$$

From equations (ii) and (iii)

$$\frac{2s}{g(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta)} = 2\left(\frac{2s}{g\sin\theta}\right)$$

$$\frac{1}{\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta} = \frac{2}{\sin\theta}$$

$$\sin\theta = 2(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta)$$

$$\sin\theta = 2\sin\theta - 2\mu\cos\theta$$

$$2\mu\cos\theta = 2\sin\theta - \sin\theta$$

$$2\mu\cos\theta = \sin\theta$$

$$\mu = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\tan\theta$$

The inclination angle is given as $\theta = 45^\circ$.

$$\mu = \frac{1}{2} \times \tan 45^\circ = \frac{1}{2} \times 1 = \frac{1}{2}$$

Therefore, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the object and the inline is $\frac{1}{2}$. Thus, the correct option is (C).

en.content: A horizontal force of 100 N is necessary to just hold a block stationary against a wall. The coefficient of friction between the block and the wall is 0.2. The weight of the block is
en.explanation:
When an object is pressed against a vertical wall by a horizontal force, it experiences forces in both the horizontal and vertical directions.

The external pushing force ($F$) acts horizontally toward the wall. The wall exerts an equal and opposite normal reaction force ($N$) directed away from the wall to prevent the block from moving through it.

Since the block does not move horizontally, these forces must be balanced:

$$N = F \, ...\,(i)$$

The Earth exerts a downward gravitational force, which is the weight ($W$) of the block.

To prevent the block from sliding down the wall, a resistive static friction force ($f_s$) acts vertically upward parallel to the contact surface.

For the block to remain stationary, the upward friction force must balance the downward weight:

$$f_s = W \, ...\,(ii)$$

Friction between two surfaces has a maximum possible threshold called the limiting static friction force ($f_{s,\max}$).

$$f_{s,\max} = \mu N \, ...\,(iii)$$

At equilibrium along vertical direction,

$$f_s = f_{s,\max}$$

$$W = \mu N$$

$$W = \mu F$$

The given horizontal force is $F = 100\,\mathrm{N}$, and the coefficient of friction is $\mu = 0.2$

$$W = 0.2 \times 100\,\mathrm{N}$$

$$W = 20\,\mathrm{N}$$

Therefore, the weight of the block is $20\,\mathrm{N}$. Thus, the correct option is (B).

en.content: The upper half of an incline plane with inclination $\theta$ is perfectly smooth while the lower half is rough. A body starting from rest at the top will again come to rest at the bottom, if the coefficient of friction for the lower half is given by
en.explanation:
Let the total length of the inclined plane be $2 s$ where upper smooth half has a length of $s$ and the lower rough half has a length of $s$.

The block starts from rest at the top, so its initial velocity is $u = 0$.

It accelerates down the smooth half, reaching a maximum velocity $v$ at the midpoint. Then, entering the rough half, friction opposes the motion, causing the block to decelerate and come to rest again at the bottom, making its final velocity $v_f = 0$.

On the upper half, there is no friction. The only force acting on the body of mass $m$ parallel to the incline is the downward component of its weight:

$$F_1 = mg \sin \theta$$

Using Newton's second law ($F_1 = ma_1$), the acceleration $a_1$ on this smooth section is:

$$ma_1 = mg \sin \theta \Rightarrow a_1 = g \sin \theta$$

Let $v$ be the velocity of the body when it reaches the midpoint (end of the smooth half).

Applying the kinematic equation with initial velocity $u = 0$ over a distance $s$:

$$v^2 = 0^2 + 2a_1s$$

$$v^2 = 2(g \sin \theta)s \ldots (i)$$

On the lower rough half, the surface exerts a normal reaction force perpendicular to the incline:

$$N = mg \cos \theta$$

The kinetic friction force acting up the incline to oppose the downward motion:

$$f_k = \mu N = \mu mg \cos \theta$$

The net force acting on the body down the incline is,

$$F_2 = mg \sin \theta - \mu mg \cos \theta$$

By Newton's second law ($F_2 = m a_2$), the acceleration $a_2$ on this rough section is:

$$m a_2 = mg \sin \theta - \mu m g \cos \theta \Rightarrow a_2 = g \sin \theta - \mu g \cos \theta$$

For this second half the initial velocity is $v$ (from the midpoint) and the final velocity at the bottom is $v_f = 0$

over a distance $s$.

Applying the kinematic equation:

$$v_f^2 = v^2 + 2 a_2 s$$

$$0 = v^2 + 2 g(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)s$$

$$v^2 = -2 g(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)s \ldots (ii)$$

From both the equations,

$$2(g \sin \theta)s = -2 g(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)s$$

$$\sin \theta = -(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)$$

$$\sin \theta = -\sin \theta + \mu \cos \theta$$

$$\sin \theta + \sin \theta = \mu \cos \theta$$

$$2 \sin \theta = \mu \cos \theta$$

$$\mu = \frac{2 \sin \theta}{\cos \theta}$$

$$\mu = 2 \tan \theta$$

Therefore, the coefficient of friction for the lower half is $2 \tan \theta$. Thus, the correct option is (A).

en.content: The force (along incline) required to just move a body up the inclined plane is double the force required to just prevent the body from sliding down the plane. The coefficient of friction is $\mu$. The inclination of the plane is
en.explanation:
When a body of mass $m$ rests on an incline of angle $\theta$, the component of its weight acting down the incline is $\mathrm{mg} \sin \theta$, and the normal force pressing against the incline is $\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{mg} \cos \theta$.

The maximum static friction between the surfaces in contact is :

$$ \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{s}}=\mu \mathrm{N}=\mu \mathrm{mg} \cos \theta $$

To push the body up the incline, the applied force $\mathrm{F}_1$ must overcome the downward component of gravity $(\mathrm{mg} \sin \theta)$ and the friction force $\left(\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{s}}\right)$, which acts down the incline to oppose the possible upward motion.

$$F_1 = mg \, \sin \theta + f_s$$

$$F_1 = mg \, \sin \theta + \mu \, mg \, \cos \theta$$

$$F_1 = mg(\sin \theta + \mu \, \cos \theta) \ldots (i)$$

If no external force is applied and $\tan \theta > \mu$, the body wants to slide down due to gravity ($mg \, \sin \theta$). In this case, friction ($f_s$) acts up the incline.

To just prevent it from sliding down, an external upward force $F_2$ is applied.

$$F_2 + f_s = mg \sin \theta$$

$$F_2 = mg \sin \theta - f_s$$

$$F_2 = mg \sin \theta - \mu mg \cos \theta$$

$$F_2 = mg(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta) \ldots (ii)$$

It is given that the force required to move the body up ($F_1$) is double the force required to prevent it from sliding ($F_2$):

$$F_1 = 2F_2$$

$$mg(\sin \theta + \mu \cos \theta) = 2\left[mg(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)\right]$$

$$\sin \theta + \mu \cos \theta = 2\left[\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta\right]$$

$$\sin \theta + \mu \cos \theta = 2\sin \theta - 2\mu \cos \theta$$

$$\mu \cos \theta + 2\mu \cos \theta = 2\sin \theta - \sin \theta$$

$$3\mu \cos \theta = \sin \theta$$

$$3\mu = \frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta}$$

$$\tan \theta = 3\mu$$

$$\theta = \tan^{-1}(3\mu)$$

Therefore, the angle of inclination is $\theta = \tan^{-1}(3\mu)$, Thus, the correct option is (D).

en.content: What is the maximum value of the force F such that the block shown in the arrangement, does not move?
en.explanation:
When a force $F$ is applied to a block at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ relative to the horizontal surface,

The horizontal component parallel to the ground is $F_x = F \cos 60^{\circ}$

The vertical component perpendicular to the ground is $F_y = F \sin 60^{\circ}$

The upward normal reaction force exerted by the ground is $N$

The downward gravitational force (weight of the block) is $mg$

The downward vertical component of the applied force is $F \sin 60^{\circ}$

The block remains vertically equilibrium on the horizontal floor, $\sum F_y = 0$

$$N = mg + F \sin 60^{\circ}$$

Friction opposes the tendency of the block to slide horizontally. The maximum value of static friction that the surface can apply before the block begins to move is the limiting static friction ($f_{s,\max}$).

$$f_{\max} = \mu N$$

$$f_{\max} = \mu (mg + F \sin 60^{\circ})$$

For the block to remain stationary, the horizontal component of the pulling force trying to move it forward ($F_x$) must be less than or equal to the maximum available opposing friction force ($f_{\max}$).

$$F \cos 60^{\circ} = \mu (mg + F \sin 60^{\circ})$$

The mass of the block is $m = \sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{kg}$, friction coefficient is $\mu = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$

$$F\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\left(\sqrt{3} \times 10 + F \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$$

$$F = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\left(10\sqrt{3} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}F\right)$$

$$F = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \times 10\sqrt{3}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}F\right)$$

$$F = 10 + \frac{1}{2}F$$

$$F - \frac{1}{2}F = 10$$

$$\frac{1}{2}F = 10$$

$$F = 20\,\mathrm{N}$$

Therefore, the maximum value of the force $F$ such that the block does not move is $20\,\mathrm{N}$. Hence, the correct option is (A).

en.content: Two blocks A and B of masses 6 kg and 3 kg rest on a frictionless horizontal surface as shown in the figure. If coefficient of friction between A and B is 0.8 and between A and ground is 0.1, then the maximum horizontal force which can make them move without separation is
en.explanation:
The external force F is applied horizontally to the upper block $\mathrm{B}\left(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}=3 \mathrm{~kg}\right)$.

When block B is pulled to the right, it tries to slide over block A . This relative sliding motion creates a static friction force $\left(f_{A B}\right)$ between their contact surfaces.

According to Newton's third law, this friction force acts in opposite directions on each block: It acts toward the left on block B to oppose its forward motion. It acts toward the right on block A, acting as driving force responsible for moving block A forward.

At the same time, the ground is rough with a friction coefficient of, which produces a friction force $\left(f_{g A}\right)$ to the the left that opposes the motion of block A.

For the blocks to move together without separating, both must have same acceleration (a).

For the block $B$ along vertical direction the normal reaction force between block $B$ and block $A\left(N_{A B}\right)$, is due to the weight of block $B$ :

$$ \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{AB}}=\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{~g}=3 \times 10=30 \mathrm{~N} $$

The maximum static friction that can develop between blocks A and B is:

$$ \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{AB}, \max }=\mu_{\mathrm{AB}} \mathrm{~N}_{\mathrm{AB}}=0.8 \times 30=24 \mathrm{~N} $$

For the block A along vertical direction,

$$ \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{gA}}=\left(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}+\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}\right) \mathrm{g}=(6+3) \times 10=90 \mathrm{~N} $$

The kinetic friction force opposing the system at the ground is:

$$ \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{gA}}=\mu_{\text {ground }} \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{gA}}=0.1 \times 90=9 \mathrm{~N} $$

Using Newton's second law for block A, the net forward force accelerating block A is,

$$ \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{AB}}-\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{gA}}=\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{a} $$

Since block A accelerate with maximum possible acceleration ($a_{\max}$) when this contact friction reaches its limiting friction ($f_{AB,\max} = 24\ \mathrm{N}$):

$$24 - 9 = 6a_{\max}$$

$$15 = 6a_{\max}$$

$$a_{\max} = \frac{15}{6} = 2.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$

If the system accelerates with value just greater than $2.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, the friction between the blocks will fail to keep up, and block B will slide relative to block A.

Let the system $(m_A + m_B)$ moving together at this maximum acceleration the net external force is,

$$F - f_{gA} = (m_A + m_B)a_{\max}$$

$$F - 9 = (6 + 3) \times 2.5$$

$$F - 9 = 9 \times 2.5$$

$$F - 9 = 22.5$$

$$F = 22.5 + 9 = 31.5\ \mathrm{N}$$

Therefore, the correct option is (B).

en.content: A wedge with a rough groove in the shape of a quarter of a circle is kept on a smooth table (see figure). A disc is placed in the groove with a small clearance. Friction exists between groove and disc. The wedge is moved with an acceleration $\sqrt{3} \mathrm{~g}$. If disc is to remain stationary relative to groove, the minimum coefficient of friction required is $\sqrt{\frac{18}{n}}$, then find $n$.
en.explanation:
The wedge accelerates horizontally to the right with an acceleration $\mathrm{a}=\sqrt{3} \mathrm{~g}$.

Because the frame is non-inertial, a pseudo force must be applied to the disc. The magnitude of this pseudo force is ma, and its direction is opposite to the acceleration of the wedge (horizontally to the left):

$$ \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{m}(\sqrt{3} \mathrm{~g})=\sqrt{3} \mathrm{mg} $$

Let the position of the disc in the circular groove be at angle $\theta$ with the vertical line passing through the centre of the arc.

The radial direction is perpendicular to the groove's surface and tangential direction is parallel to the groove's surface.

Radial component of gravitational force is $mg\cos\theta$

Tangential component gravitational force acting down along the curve is $mg\sin\theta$

Radial component of pseudo force is $\sqrt{3}mg\sin\theta$

Tangential component pseudo force acting up along the curve is $\sqrt{3}mg\cos\theta$

Since there is no motion in the radial direction, the normal reaction force $N$ exerted by the track balances the radial components:

$$N = mg\cos\theta + \sqrt{3}mg\sin\theta = mg(\cos\theta + \sqrt{3}\sin\theta)$$

For the minimum coefficient of friction to be found at the point of slipping, the net tangential force must be zero.

$$F_{\text{tangential}} = \left|\sqrt{3}mg\cos\theta - mg\sin\theta\right| = mg\left|\sqrt{3}\cos\theta - \sin\theta\right|$$

For equilibrium,

$$f_s = F_{\text{tangential}}$$

$$\Rightarrow \mu N \geq F_{\text{tangential}} = mg\left|\sqrt{3}\cos\theta - \sin\theta\right|$$

$$\Rightarrow \mu\left[mg(\cos\theta + \sqrt{3}\sin\theta)\right] = mg\left|\sqrt{3}\cos\theta - \sin\theta\right|$$

$$\Rightarrow \mu \geq \frac{\left|\sqrt{3}\cos\theta - \sin\theta\right|}{\cos\theta + \sqrt{3}\sin\theta}$$

For minimum coefficient of friction required for the block to remain stationary we need to find the maximum value of the function

$$f(\theta) = \frac{\sqrt{3}\cos\theta - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta + \sqrt{3}\sin\theta}$$

$$f(\theta) = \frac{\sqrt{3} - \tan\theta}{1 + \sqrt{3}\tan\theta} = \frac{\tan 60^\circ - \tan\theta}{1 + \tan 60^\circ\tan\theta}$$

$$\Rightarrow f(\theta) = \tan(60^\circ - \theta)$$

For the required position the angle with vertical is $\theta = 30^\circ$.

$$\mu = \tan(60^\circ - 30^\circ) = \tan 30^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$$

$$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{\frac{18}{n}} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{3} = \frac{18}{n}$$

$$n = 18 \times 3 = 54$$

Therefore, the value of n is 54.

en.content: The following figure shows an accelerating conveyor belt inclined at an angle $37^{\circ}$ above horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the belt and block is 1 . Find the least time (in second) in which block can reach the top, starting from rest at the bottom.
en.explanation:
When a block is placed on an upward-moving conveyor belt, the component of gravity acting parallel to the incline pulls the block downward

$$ \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{g} \|}=\mathrm{mg} \sin \theta $$

To make the block move upward, the conveyor belt must exert an upward static friction force ( $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{s}}$ ) on the block. Along the direction perpendicular to the incline the normal force balances the gravity component:

$$ \mathrm{N}=\mathrm{mg} \cos 37^{\circ} $$

Along the direction parallel to the incline the net force is,

$$ \mathrm{F}_{\text {net }}=\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{s}}-\mathrm{mg} \sin 37^{\circ} $$

According to Newton's second law ( $\mathrm{F}_{\text {net }}=\mathrm{ma}$ ), the acceleration is:

$$ \mathrm{ma}=\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{s}}-\mathrm{mg} \sin 37^{\circ} \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=\frac{\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{s}}}{\mathrm{~m}}-\mathrm{g} \sin 37^{\circ} $$

The maximum possible acceleration for the least travel time, the static friction force must be maximum limiting value $\left(\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{s}, \text { max }}=\mu \mathrm{N}\right)$ :

$$ \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{s}}=\mu\left(\mathrm{mg} \cos 37^{\circ}\right) $$

From the expression of acceleration,

$$a_{\max}=\frac{\mu mg\cos 37^\circ}{m}-g\sin 37^\circ$$

$$a_{\max}=g(\mu \cos 37^\circ-\sin 37^\circ)$$

$$a_{\max}=10\times\left(1\times\frac{4}{5}-\frac{3}{5}\right)$$

$$a_{\max}=10\times(0.8-0.6)$$

$$a_{\max}=10\times0.2=2\ \mathrm{m/s}^2$$

The block starts from rest ($u=0$) at the bottom and needs to cover a total distance of $s=4\ \mathrm{m}$ along the incline to reach the top.

Using the second kinematic equation of motion:

$$s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^2$$

$$4=0+\frac{1}{2}\times2\times t^2$$

$$4=t^2$$

$$t=\sqrt{4}=2\ \text{seconds}$$

Therefore, the time taken to reach the top is 2 seconds.

en.content: Blocks $A$ and $B$ shown each has mass 10 kg . If coefficient of static friction between $A$ and $B$ is 0.3 and that between $B$ and incline is 0.4 , then what is the value of force $P$ (in $N$ ) to just start the motion of $B$ ? $\left(\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)$
en.explanation:
Both blocks A and B have an equal mass of $\mathrm{m}=10 \mathrm{~kg}$.

The angle of inclination is given as $\theta=37^{\circ}$.

The parallel component of weight down the incline is,

$$F_{g\parallel}=mg\sin 37^{\circ}=10\times 10\times 0.6\,\text{N}=60\,\text{N}$$

The perpendicular component of weight into the inclined surface is,

$$F_{g\perp}=mg\cos 37^{\circ}=10\times 10\times 0.8\,\text{N}=80\,\text{N}$$

The normal reaction force $N_1$ between A and B supports only the perpendicular component of block A:

$$N_1=mg\cos 37^{\circ}=80\,\text{N}$$

The coefficient of friction is $\mu_1=0.3$, the maximum static friction force at this surface is:

$$f_{1,\max}=\mu_1N_1=0.3\times 80=24\,\text{N}$$

The normal reaction force $N_2$ exerted by the incline balances the combined perpendicular components of both blocks A and B:

$$N_2=N_1+m_Bg\cos 37^{\circ}=80+80=160\,\text{N}$$

The coefficient of friction $\mu_2=0.4$, the maximum static friction force at this surface is:

$$f_{2,\max}=\mu_2N_2=0.4\times 160=64\,\text{N}$$

The force P is pulling block B down the incline. Block A is connected to a wall by a string parallel to the incline. As block B moves downward under the pulling force $P$, it tries to drag block A along with it.

Block A is connected by the string, so block A remains stationary relative to the incline surface.

Therefore, relative motion occurs at both interfaces, block B slides down relative to block A, and block B slides down relative to the incline.

The external pulling force acting downward along the incline is P

The downward component of block B's own weight $F_{gB\parallel} = m_B g \sin 37^{\circ} = 10 \times 10 \times \frac{3}{5} = 60\ \text{N}$

The maximum friction force from the stationary block A opposing block B's downward motion is,

$$f_{1,\max} = 24\ \text{N}$$

The maximum friction force from the incline surface opposing block B's downward motion is,

$$f_{2,\max} = 64\ \text{N}$$

For block B to just begin moving downward, the total downward pulling forces must balance the total maximum resisting forces up the incline:

$$P + mg \sin 37^{\circ} = f_{1,\max} + f_{2,\max}$$

$$P + 60 = 24 + 64$$

$$P + 60 = 88$$

$$P = 88 - 60 = 28\ \text{N}$$

Therefore, the required value of P to just start the motion of B is $28\ \text{N}$.

en.content: The friction coefficient between the board and the floor shown in figure is 0.5 . Find the maximum force (in newton) that the man can exert on the rope, so that the board does not slip on the floor.
en.explanation:
The mass of the man is $M=60 \mathrm{~kg}$ and the mass of the board is $m=15 \mathrm{~kg}$.

The friction coefficient between the board and the floor is $\mu=0.5$.

The man pulls the rope downward with a tension force T. By Newton's third law, the rope pulls upward on the man with an equal force T .

For the massless and inextensible string, the tension throughout the length is same.

Since the rope attaches horizontally to the board, the same tension T pulls horizontally to the right on the board.

For the Man:

Downward gravitational force (his weight) is $W_M = Mg$

Upward tension from the rope he is holding is $T$

Upward normal force exerted by the board on his feet $N_1$

Since he is in vertical equilibrium:

$$N_1 + T = Mg \Rightarrow N_1 = Mg - T$$

For the Board:

Downward gravitational force (its own weight) $W_m = mg$

Downward normal force from the man's feet (action-reaction pair) $N_1$

Upward normal force exerted by the floor on the board $N_f$

Since the board is in vertical equilibrium:

$$N_f = mg + N_1$$

$$N_f = mg + (Mg - T) = (M + m)g - T$$

A forward pulling force due to the tension in the rope attached to it $T$.

A backward resisting static friction force from the floor $f_s$.

For the board to remain stationary without slipping, the horizontal pulling force must not exceed the maximum possible static friction force that the floor can provide:

$$T \leq f_{s,\max} \Rightarrow T \leq \mu N_f$$

$$T \leq \mu[(M + m)g - T] \Rightarrow T \leq \mu(M + m)g - \mu T$$

$$\Rightarrow T + \mu T \leq \mu(M + m)g \Rightarrow T(1 + \mu) \leq \mu(M + m)g$$

$$\Rightarrow T \leq \frac{\mu(M + m)g}{1 + \mu} \Rightarrow T_{\max} = \frac{\mu(M + m)g}{1 + \mu}$$

Using $M = 60\ \mathrm{kg}$, $m = 15\ \mathrm{kg}$, $\mu = 0.5$, and taking $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$:

$$T_{\max} = \frac{0.5 \times (60 + 15) \times 10}{1 + 0.5} = \frac{0.5 \times 75 \times 10}{1.5}$$

$$T_{\max} = \frac{375}{1.5} = 250\ \mathrm{N}$$

Therefore, the maximum force applied by man is $250\ \mathrm{N}.$

en.content: A man can just push a box on $37^{\circ}$ concrete slope. When he keeps it at the point, where the angle increases to $53^{\circ}$, he can just hold it from sliding back. If the coefficient of friction between the box and the concrete slope is $\mu$, find $\frac{1}{\mu}$. Assume that the man is applying same magnitude of force along the tangent to the curve only.
en.explanation:
When an object of mass m is placed on a rough inclined plane of angle $\theta$, the normal reaction force N perpendicular to the incline is :

$$ \mathrm{N}=\mathrm{mg} \cos \theta $$

The maximum limiting static friction force ( $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{s}}$ ) available to oppose relative motion is :

$$ \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{s}}=\mu \mathrm{N}=\mu \mathrm{mg} \cos \theta $$

The gravitational force component down parallel to the incline is :

$$ \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{g}}=\mathrm{mg} \sin \theta $$

Case 1 : Pushing the box up a $37^{\circ}$ slope

When the man pushes the box up the incline of $\theta_1 = 37^\circ$, the friction force acts in the downward direction to oppose this upward motion. Therefore, the man's force (F) must overcome both the downward gravity component and the downward friction force:

$$F = mg \sin \theta_1 + \mu mg \cos \theta_1$$

$$F = mg(\sin 37^\circ + \mu \cos 37^\circ) \ldots (i)$$

Case 2 : Holding the box from sliding down a $53^\circ$ slope

When the box is on a slope of $\theta_2 = 53^\circ$, it tends to slide down under its own weight. To prevent it from sliding down the incline, the man applies the same force $F$ up the incline. Static friction helps the man by acting upward along the incline to oppose the downward sliding tendency.

For equilibrium condition,

$$F + \mu mg \cos \theta_2 = mg \sin \theta_2$$

$$F = mg \sin \theta_2 - \mu mg \cos \theta_2$$

$$F = mg(\sin 53^\circ - \mu \cos 53^\circ)\ \ldots\ (\mathrm{ii})$$

Since the magnitude of the force $F$ applied by the man is same in both cases,

$$mg(\sin 37^\circ + \mu \cos 37^\circ) = mg(\sin 53^\circ - \mu \cos 53^\circ)$$

$$\sin 37^\circ + \mu \cos 37^\circ = \sin 53^\circ - \mu \cos 53^\circ$$

$$\frac{3}{5} + \mu \left(\frac{4}{5}\right) = \frac{4}{5} - \mu \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)$$

$$3 + 4\mu = 4 - 3\mu$$

$$4\mu + 3\mu = 4 - 3$$

$$7\mu = 1$$

$$\mu = \frac{1}{7}$$

Therefore, the value of $\frac{1}{\mu}$ is $7$.
